blocks.x: Okay, I'll mention here first of all, the date is April the 6th, 1961. We're down at 731 St. Peter's Street. This is Bill Russell interviewing Jerry Blumberg. Do you mind giving your full name and your birth date, where you were born and so on? My full name is Gerald Herschel.
We were talking about the Stuyvesant, about your trips back and forth to Baltimore. When did you decide to go up there and study, take lessons and all of it, Bun?

Well, Kratka was saying that I ought to move to New York. He wanted to get together this band he had in mind. So he invited me to stay at his family's place until I got a place of my own, and so I did move up. With my parents' permission this time, and stayed with the Kratkas, I guess, for several weeks. And finally, I got a place down in the village, a little room that was being leased by Jan Kindler. He was just hanging on to it because it was still under rent control, and the rent was real cheap. And it was a nice little extra room, so he let me use that room for a while.
By the way, what ever happened to Kindler in the book he was writing? You know anything about it?
I don't know anything about it. I think he finished it, and it was supposed to have been pretty good, but I don't know about the publication.

I never did know what happened to him. I know one funny thing that happened one day, he wanted to get Bunks' reaction to Jelly Rolls' Library of Congress records. He'd gotten a few of them that Lomax or somebody had given him tests, which Lomax really wasn't supposed to give out. I gave some later to Charles Smith and I, too, and then Spivak, the head of the department, found out about it and stopped it right in the middle of the series, or after we had about two-thirds. But anyway, one day he brought those up to play for Bunks. He wanted to get his reactions and see what Bunks had to say about Jelly. He was going to write it up in his book or something, I guess, in the chapter on Jelly Roll or something. So he got Bunks sitting down and stuff in Gene's apartment. And before the first number was over, Bunks was sound asleep. He never heard of nobody, never got one word out of Bunks. That's all he was interested in hearing Jelly. Go ahead. You're talking about him. Every time I think of him, I think of that little Bunks story. It's frustrating. Yeah.
Yeah, well, of course, when I moved up to New York, I think the Stuyvesant engagement was over already. That ended about the 10th or so. Well, this was the second.
I didn't move up, I think, until after the second one was over. The second one, when Don was there.

Yeah. Did you get up to hear the band with Don? Oh, yeah, I came up to hear the band with Don, and that was very exciting, too, because Don was playing exceptionally well with the band, and Kratka and I and a few others used to stand behind the piano there and just listen to the piano, which was very exciting, some very exciting Jelly Roll style.
Yeah, Don was playing more Jelly Roll style then than he does now.

Yeah. Yeah. And Bunk was very pleased with Don. He used to get up and walk around and stand beside the piano and play a solo, which before that he had never made very much of a point of playing solos, I don't think. I mean, he had certain solos he'd do in certain numbers, but he'd just stand up and do them. He really tried to do a little more with setting off his solos as apart from the ensembles. When Don was with the band, he'd go over and stand next to the piano and do a real solo type solo and very pretty things. You didn't move up then? I didn't move up until after that was over.

That second engagement, if I remember rightly, was the only one when Maude was up there, too. There was something you were telling the other night, the time when Maude was at the table. I forget what the story is now, but you were there once when she was there in New York, too.

Yeah, well, I was telling a couple stories the other night, happening to be at the Stuyvesant when there was conflict in the band, when Bunk was having trouble with a drummer. And I guess I get Bunk actually had trouble with both drummers, Baby and Steel.
I know, even Kaiser Marshall, too.
Yeah. I mean, he was with the band one time.
They didn't, I don't know, Bunk was sort of particular about his drummers, I guess. Well, drummers are a problem. Yeah.
But I remember Bunk turning around and beating on the bass drum with his horn to try to get the kind of beat he wanted at times there.
I know Bunk used to object to what he called the iron foundry. He had his baby's cymbal was right in the back of his head about within those six inches almost.
Oh, that can be.
Yeah, and he used to speak of it all the kitchenware he'd talk about sometimes in the iron foundry, you'd call it.
Well, yeah, that can be, I mean, it gets to the point where that's all you can hear is the cymbal. But it's just a question of rearranging the furniture, I guess. I don't know.

In the old style, New Orleans seating, they always had the drums on one end, so it wouldn't be right back at the trumpeter's head. He'd be separated with the trombonist in there between the drum and the coronet. Go ahead if you can go ahead with your lessons pretty soon. I mean, that's something else before that.

I'd like to talk a little about Bunk. I mean, my impression of Bunk as he looked. I mean, I remember the band, of course, was all sitting down. The whole band had a marvelous look about it. Lawrence Marrero looked like a real rock of Gibraltar sitting there playing the banjo. I remember he looked like the steadiest beat in town, you know. Even if you didn't hear him, you knew that the guy had to have a steady beat because he absolutely had this immobile smile, a Buddha-like smile. And he was a great-looking fellow. And, of course, the horn players were sitting down in chairs behind their stands, and Bunk was wearing these high shoes. And he'd have his pants hiked up so you could see all these high shoes he wore and his long underwear. Yeah, long underwear in there. Always in the summer, I think, too. Yeah. I think so. And Bunk had a way of cocking his eyes over to one corner of the room when he'd play. He'd usually be looking up at a corner. Louis does very much the same thing. And it gave him a great look and went with the sound of the horn. But, I mean, a very striking stare. You'd really be seeing some eyeball there. Yeah. It would come along with the playing. And when he'd play a climbing phrase, an ascending phrase, his eyes would go up, you know, which would add to the effect of the whole thing. And he had a very interesting way. Well, he used to run the band very authoritatively. There was no doubt that he was running the band when you'd see him because he'd stomp his feet very loud, you know, to stomp off the tune, set the tempo.
Had you ever heard that anyplace else before?
No, I don't think I'd ever heard a scene that way of running a band with the pounding of the foot. And he would take the thing out with one pound of the foot.
We were talking the other night about you thought it's usually in the middle of the last chorus before the...
I think it depended on probably when he would decide to take the thing out. I think it would either be right before the last chorus.
That's what I thought usually. I would think that's the place they usually should give it and they're supposed to. But I think, too, sometimes they'd bunk and other people, too, in the middle of it.

There'd be a last-minute decision to take the thing out. And there'd be a pause between phrases and you'd hear this bang, you know. And bunk would kind of move his head when he'd stomp his foot, too. Kind of a twist, throw of the head like a, I don't know, I think of a thoroughbred horse gives a little throw of the head and a snort, you know. And bunk had a way of throwing his head just like that, you know. And he'd stomp his foot, he'd throw that one foot down and give his head that little throw, you know. And then play the thing out. And he had a wonderful way of running the band. When the crowd would be particularly pleased by a tune, if it was a fast tune, an exciting tune, he'd just stomp, as soon as the tune would be over and the people would start applauding, he'd stomp it off and start playing the same tune all over again. And I don't know if that's common practice down here.

Yeah, it always has been down here, I think. And still is, to some extent, if you've got a real New Orleans old-time group there, they'll have to play a tune twice again. Dances, maybe not so much at some of the nightclubs and sessions around.
Yeah, yeah.
Regular dance, they'll play them twice.
I remember that was a real surprise the first time.
They did that practically everything, because the crowd up there liked everything.
Yeah.
I think they'd applaud. Sometimes they'd go three, I've heard them three or four times on certain numbers.

Yeah, they'd go good on three or four times. They'd go right into what would correspond to maybe the third chorus from the last again, and then they'd take it two more out or something like that. And he would pace the band very well. He'd build up. He wouldn't let the band, I think, achieve too great an excitement early in the evening. He'd pace it. If the tunes were swinging along real well, but it was early in the evening, he'd kind of cut them short a little bit. So there'd be something left for later on. And I remember noticing that, how the thing seemed to build from the beginning of the evening right all the way through. It just kept getting more and more exciting each set. And you never got the feeling that the band was going downhill after a climax. It always seemed to be getting better. And that's when I realized that I had been listening to too many records and not enough in-person performances, because you can't get that concept of a band over the whole period of an evening from one tune on a record.
Is there anything else while we're speaking about hearing Bunk about his tone that you can describe or that impressed you?

Well, it was absolutely clear. Not only his tone. In the first place, he had the kind of tone that was so beautiful that no matter what he had played, it would have sounded great. I mean, that's the way I felt about it. I could have heard him play scales, and it would have been just as thrilling to me. But everything about his playing, his attack, was beautifully precise. And his slurs were very precise. And he would change his tone. He would soften it down. And it would get more and less piercing as he wanted to use it that way. And he had beautiful control, in other words, over the different kinds of sounds he could get out of the horn. And, I mean, of course, this is when he was at his strongest. Now, there were nights when he wasn't in such good shape. His lip was a little weak, and it wasn't this fine. Of course, Bunk just about always got a beautiful sound out of the horn. There were a few times when he wasn't playing well.
Yeah, unless he just didn't want to play or had been drinking.
Yeah, when he'd been drinking or something like that.
He'd be drinking when he didn't feel right and things were going wrong and he didn't care what he did sometime. But even then, like you say, it never did anything in bad taste.
Yeah, the sound was always there.
If he could blow it all, it was something to hear, yeah. But there were some nights, of course, where you could understand why some people wouldn't be so impressed with him, too.
Yeah, well, that's a trouble. A lot of the people around New York happened to come in on the night when Bunk was sitting up there practically snoring. Yeah.

I can remember that one picture. There's a famous picture that Ouija took, I believe, published in one of his books, where Bunk is sound asleep and slept after the first, maybe, set or the second set anyway. He went to sleep on the stand and sat there until the whole dance was over. And Wild Bill happened to be there and he played and sat within about a yard of him, blowing right straight at him just for fun or for meanness or something. And Bunk never heard him. I'm sure it wasn't just entirely an act, although as soon as it was over, Bunk gets up and goes home plenty quick. And I don't think he staggered home or anything else either. But still, if he didn't want to play, like in Boston, that same thing that came up with Sidney Bechet, he didn't like the band. And he'd sit there all night long rubbing his lip. He had six or seven kinds of medicine all over his music stand. He'd always have his music stand up there. He'd rub some sort of like camphor, different, you know, stuff on there.
He used tincture of myrrh. That's what he gave me a bottle. What was that? And I had a bottle up until recently, the bottle he gave me.
Dr. Tischner's, what do they call it? Antiseptic is one of his favorites. They all use that.
Well, maybe it's the same thing.
Dr. Tischner's a building down here on Canal Street, a big white building right near the ferry boat.
I think it might be the same thing as tincture of myrrh. I'm not sure. I don't know. This is just a clear thing.
It had a lot of alcohol in it. They used to drink during Prohibition.
Oh, yeah. No, that's something else.

I know in Chicago once when I had a tooth pulled, I was down at Mahalia's. And Mahalia and all of her other relatives and different people there, oh, get some Dr. Tischner's ointment and put that in your tooth. Anything that goes wrong at all, they use Dr. Tischner's for. And Bunk always had a bottle of that. But he'd have all these medicines on his music stand, and he'd sit there sometime for two or three sets. I don't think he'd play one piece. Honestly, he'd sit there all night long rubbing that. But any time he wanted to, though, if he'd feel like it and wanted to show us that he could play, we'd go up there once. I went up from Pittsburgh once to Boston to hear him one weekend. Occasionally, about once every set, maybe he'd get his horn out and really blow. He could blow good. And then maybe a broadcast would come on and he'd blow pretty good for that, too, for a set real late at night. But most of the time he'd be sitting there putting on this act or something. And yet his lip wasn't that bad. Go ahead now. We were talking about your impression of hearing and his tone.

Yeah, well, he'd hit notes like he'd crack a whip. It was just beautiful precision and cleanliness about his playing. And he played a very buoyant style, kind of bouncy, I guess you'd call it. I don't know. It's pretty hard to really... Yeah, I know it's hard to describe any style. Just put it all into words.
Is there anything else about the way he'd sit around? I noticed he'd always sit like he was quite relaxed.

Yeah. Yeah, I remember sometimes... Well, he was always leafing through his music. He had a big stack of lead sheets up there of all these different tunes. And he'd be sitting there sometimes playing, holding the horn up with one hand. And it didn't make any difference to him whether it was the right hand or the left hand. He'd just... Sometimes he'd play through a couple choruses with his left hand, holding the horn and fingering it with the left hand, which isn't an exceptionally difficult thing. But it didn't seem to bother... He didn't even seem to be aware of it, you know. And he'd be leafing through the music with his right hand and reaching around for things.

I can remember one night. That's about the second or third week the band first opened there. And the Metronome editor, Simon, or whoever his name was, went to Leonard Feather. And there's two or three other people from Metronome, I think, were there. Not Feather, but some other people. And Bunk sort of put on an act for him. He'd play with one hand. I guess his right hand. He'd hold the horn with the right hand and the finger. And he'd be buttoning his coat.
He was always doing things like that. So he could play with one hand.
He'd be buttoning his coat and fixing his handkerchief or something in a pocket. And always busy with that other hand doing things to show.
So some of that was an act, too. Yeah, sure.
Although ordinarily he didn't care anything about showmanship, as you know. It was strictly the music.
Yeah. Except that in his way, he was a fine showman. Yeah, that's right. He consistently presented a very exciting image to go along with the playing. Yeah. A lean, very lean fella. And...
Yeah, and before the band opened, for instance, he asked to get the music stands all fixed up with the names painted on and little crowns painted on.
He had ideas, too.
I mean, it wasn't that he just didn't care how the looks. I don't mean that. The music, of course, was a big thing with him, naturally. That's right.

So I guess I might have approached him at that time about lessons. I don't recall. But anyway, when I finally moved up to New York, Monk was living up there and in between jobs, I guess, at the time. Did he stay in New York after the second engagement?

No, no, he went right back in June. His wife was there and they went back, oh, within two or three days after the Stuyvesant engagement closed. That's when he made those records with Don and the drummer.
Yeah, Steele.
Steele. And then went back about the next day or two after that, I think.
Well, anyway, he must have come back a few months later, maybe for a single concert or something.

Well, I don't think it was William. It was quite a while later, if I remember rightly. That was 1946. He went to Chicago later that year. In the fall, he went to Chicago. I don't remember that he went to New York that next fall. You don't remember your dates exactly, you say, on some of that.
No, I'm very vague about the dates.
It might have been 1947 before he got back to New York.
It could very well have been. I'm trying to remember what else was going on then, but I can't think of anything to place
it. Anyway, I have some of that in my notes pretty well dated, I think, with letters from Gene Williams and other people about his activities.
I remember one time Bunk flew up from New Orleans to play a concert for Maltz, but I think that was after that. I think that was after he went down. Unless maybe that...
That was... Yeah, that wouldn't be before 1947, hardly, I don't believe.
But anyway...
Where was Bunk living then?

Well, he was living with the Lofburrs, as I recall, most of the time. There was also a period when he was living with... Who was it? Kaiser Marshall? Yeah. Kaiser Marshall's apartment, was it? No. No. The other drummer. Not Kaiser.
Oh.
Freddie Moore. Freddie Moore's apartment. That's right.
That's the time that his wife put the... Freddie Moore's wife...
Put the padlock on the telephone, yeah. Yeah. Bunk was very offended. And I used to...
Did he tell you then? That he said...

Yeah, yeah. He told me... He said he couldn't understand why people acted like that. That all he had to do was just tell him not to use the phone, and he wouldn't use the phone. But here he was sitting in his easy chair, and the phone was right at his elbow, and this was his spot in the apartment, and there was a constant reminder that he kind of wasn't welcome, I guess, or that there was a limited welcome. Yeah. Yeah. So, but he invited me, you know, up to spend the afternoons with him. I guess this was a period when there was absolutely nothing going on, and New York has a way of forgetting about you as fast as it can get excited about you. And so at this particular time, Bunk had absolutely nothing happening, and he was just... I would go up wherever he was staying, and just find him, and it's kind of dozing off in an easy chair, looking out of the window. He almost never had any visitors, you know, during that time. Nobody even cared to go up and talk to him. Probably didn't even know he was there, actually. Yeah, probably hasn't. He probably thought he was back in New Orleans. But, uh...
If I remember rightly, I know I moved away from Pittsburgh in the spring of 1947, and I timed my leaving there to stop in Chicago when he went up for a concert or two for Skank.
Yeah.

And John Skank. And at that time, he was living with Dave Bell, and Loughborough was...if he wasn't living with Dave Bell, they were always there at the apartment. Oh. So it was after the spring of 1947. I think that must have been almost fall of 1947, before he went up there for Malts, and then that other engagement at the Stuyvesant, and the ones up there at the Caravan, and all
of those.
I think we're mostly from September on...
Well then, maybe it was Malts that brought him back to New York. Quite likely it was. For that whole period, that probably began that whole period.
He never wanted to fly. He always refused to fly.

I remember he was sick in the stomach when he got the plane just in...the plane just came in just in time to make the concert. And I remember, I don't recall where the concert was, probably Town Hall. Yeah, I think so. But I think...I know Lead Belly was there, and Danny Barker, and Simeon was there. I can remember Bunk coming in, and he looked pretty bad, and he said he felt pretty bad. He was sick, and he had an upset stomach on the airplane. And he didn't feel too good, and he wasn't playing too well at that concert either. He sounded very weak, you know. But I remember hearing them warm up. Danny Barker and Lead Belly were playing a guitar duet. They were just kind of tuning up in the dressing room as I was walking up the stairs. And they got swinging onto one of these two guitar blues things, a fast blues, and then Bunk was warming up. And so he chimed in, and a very swinging sound there in the dressing room. And I don't remember who was in the band that gave the concert. I think it was maybe Sammy Price on piano, and maybe Simeon on clarinet. I don't recall.

Nicholas was in some of those things too. Yeah. I have a postcard, I think, listing that concert. I know, I think Maud, someone told me that she had to get Bunk on the plane finally, that... I don't know what she was doing in New Orleans or how they got him on the plane, but he would never take it under his own free will, except he was the only chance he could have possibly gotten there. He probably didn't want to go to the concert in the first place. He knew it was going to be bad. Yeah. In a bad group. He always used to tell me he'd never get him on a plane. He said, whenever that engine goes bad, he said, I want to be able to get out and walk.
Yeah.
So, I don't know how they ever... I was surprised that they got him on it.
Well, apparently he wasn't in too good shape. And I don't think his horn was with him, and they had to find him a horn.
Usually he'd leave his horn, I think it was down here in a pawn shop or something, he left it down here or something at that time.
So...

When he got to New York, the very first time he got there, he got out his horn too. And we got Mooney, George Lewis's wife's brother-in-law, who finally found out where his horn was and got it, and then they mailed it up there. Oh, yeah. Yeah, well... Go ahead with the rest of that engagement. I think that was 47, though.

Yeah, I remember the concert, and I remember being kind of disappointed, and you know, the funk just felt so bad, and so forth. But anyway, those were the lessons. I mean, he invited me up to spend the afternoons with him and take lessons or what have you, you know. And I'd come up to wherever he was, and usually he was in. Every now and then he'd be out someplace. I'd have to scout around the neighborhood and look in the corner drugstore or the neighborhood bar, wherever, try to figure out where he went off to, you know. And, but sometimes we'd just sit there and talk all afternoon, wouldn't even get to play horn at all. Because actually I wasn't as interested in taking actual lessons as I was in trying to figure out what his secrets were. I mean, I heard a magic in his playing that had me all agog, you know. And I was just trying to plumb the secrets of it somehow. I was trying to figure out, had he listened a lot to Calypso music or what. I mean, there was something, some quality in his playing, a rhythmic quality that I just couldn't put my finger on. But it, it was.
Well, you mentioned the other day about that Calypso that he once went up. What was that?

Yeah, well, there was one time when, when, I guess it was one of those afternoons, I went up there and he said, well, last night I played in a little session, this was up in Harlem, in a bar down the street. And there were a bunch of West Indians there, he said, and I played, we played this tune. And he took out his horn and played some beautiful little Calypso melody that I'd never heard before or since. And I wrote it down. It was so nice, but I, I lost the paper it was written on. But I remember how striking it was. He played Calypso, I mean, that particular piece, like a, like a native Calypso player. He really had that, that feeling very, very strongly. And, and it was something that I just, uh, was trying to figure out just where his, uh, where his feet were, you know, and what, what style of music and trying to figure out how to, how to think about the man.
By the way, when you did take lessons, did he charge you for it?
Oh, no, he never, he never charged. He never charged. He told me to get this book. I guess he said either get Arbenz or the Imperial Method. And so I got the Imperial Method.
Remember where that was published or who wrote it?
I don't recall. It was published by the Church Company, the John Church Company. That's Philadelphia, I think.

And, uh... I think there maybe had been two series of Imperial Methods. I found some real old Imperial Violin and Mandolin Methods once. It might have been an older series. And Baby Dodds, if I remember rightly, had an Imperial Drum Method. Oh, is it right? He kept it for all those years. He was, he almost cried when he thought about it. He left it in the car once and took his car in for repair and somebody stole it. After keeping it ever since he was a kid here in New Orleans, took it to New York and the thing was lost or stolen up there. And he sure regretted it. I think that was Imperial. That's on the Baby Tapes. But I just wondered. I was surprised to hear that the Bunker recommended the Imperial Method.
Yeah, well, it had some tunes in the back that he liked, I think. There's one, uh... I don't know if I can even remember the name. It's, it's, uh... I think it's a quadrille or something in the back.
Was it a beginner's method? Started right at the beginning?

It started at the beginning with the whole notes, you know. And, uh, it got into a little double-tonguing. It's very much like the Arbinds, but, uh, maybe a little easier than the Arbinds. Yeah. Uh, and, uh, Bunker played several of the tunes in the back for me. Several of the, uh, these, there were, I think there was a polka in the back that he played, and a quadrille, at different times, you know. And, uh...
Did he have it memorized or played off of the music? Do you remember?

Well, he played it correctly off of the music. I don't know how well he knew. Apparently he had used this book to teach a lot. A lot, yeah, and he knew the book. Uh, he, I still have it in Baltimore with the pages marked where he marked, uh, different things for me to do.
Did he mark fingering, or did he mark the rhythm or time or counting, or what did he mark?

He marked, uh, he checked certain lines for me to practice, and he told me how to, how to beat my foot. He says to beat 4-4, except if it's a fast tune, and then beat 2-4. Yeah. And, uh, uh, I was having a lot of lip trouble at the time, uh, very weak lip. I've always had some kind of trouble like that, but at that time, particularly bad. And he was telling me to play octaves, play a lot of octaves, which, uh, later on, I've come to appreciate, is pretty good advice for this. Slurdoms? Well, both, both, uh, he said you could just play, uh, just tongue them and it would help. Tongue them, too. And, uh, uh, uh, but as I say, the lessons were very informal things, and, and, uh, there was actually very little time spent in real lessons. Yeah. Yeah. Because I would be just as interested in asking him about Jimmy Noon or something, you know, as he would be in, in, in sitting there and, and talking about Jimmy Noon. Yeah. And sometimes we just wouldn't get the horns out of the, uh, cases.
Uh, did he ever, uh, to get back to that one detail of counting, did he ever talk, insist on you stomping your foot all the time, or did he say anything about that much?

I know some pupils he had. No, there, there was just the one time when he said, this is the way you, you know, you're gonna, you're gonna play lead, you know, and, and you got to stomp off the tunes, and, uh, you know, and this is the way you, you beat your foot, you know. Mm-hmm. And, uh, he was trying to tell me how to run a band. Well, at the time I wasn't interested in learning how to run a band. I was interested in finding out what made him tick. Yeah. I mean, he was the guy that fascinated me, and I, and I guess I was less interested in taking lessons than in, and talking to him. Mm-hmm. And, uh, uh, trying to figure him out, you know. And, uh, sometimes I'd come up there, and he'd fall asleep on me, you know. Yeah. I mean, he'd be a drowsy, the apartment would be overheated. Yeah, that's happened to me. Yeah. Yeah. Plenty of people, yeah. He was the most relaxed. And he'd be sitting in an easy chair, and, and I'll never forget Bob Milkey and I went up once, and, and, uh, I guess Bunk was really sleepy. And he, uh, he was, uh, lying across the bed, and, and, uh, I don't know if he'd been drinking the night before or something, but, but, you know, we were supposed to come up and have some kind of rehearsal for, oh, that's right. It was for this, uh, this series of jobs we played with Bunk. And, and so we got up there, and he was lying across the bed, and he, he got, got up and got his horn out, I think. But he was so sleepy, he could just hardly keep his eyes open. And the next thing we knew, he had, he had suggested a couple tunes that we ought to do. I think, uh, he wanted to do, uh, Beale Street Blue.

Oh, you were talking about this rehearsal you were going to have? Yeah, the rehearsal for the Caravan. Was it the Caravan? Yeah, Mustard Van. Yeah. And we went up there, it was just Bob Mielke and myself, to talk over tunes we were going to do. And we were talking about Beale Street Blues, and Bunk sang a couple of the themes and got his horn out and played a few notes, I guess. And the next thing we knew, he was all sound asleep, and so we didn't know just what to do. We were kind of standing there, and so we tried to put his horn away for him, because he's lying there on the bed with the horn on his chest, and his hand just kind of draped over the horn lightly, bent at the wrist. And so we tried to get his horn out of his hand, and it was like a grip of iron. You know, you couldn't get the horn, you wouldn't let go of the horn, you know, and yet he was snoring away. And we were trying to get his fingers off the horn, and he just had to give up finally. It was like glue, you know. And I guess it's an old habit to hold on to your horn, all circumstances. But, so we just had to leave him there with the horn, and there were times he'd fall asleep when I was talking to him. There was one time when I visited him, he was staying at the Loughborough's apartment downtown in New York. I don't have any idea what the order of these different residences was.
It was probably later than the Freddie Moore, I think, anyway. I may have that documented someplace, too. But anyway...

Thank you, my pardon. Go ahead. I went down there, and he wasn't in the apartment, and I was scouting around the neighborhood and found him in the neighborhood bar. And there was one of these bars frequented by the rough types of the neighborhood, which was mostly truck drivers and steam fitters and people. That was over on the west side, I think, wasn't it? Yeah. Or 8th Avenue, was it? Probably was, yeah.
I think about 11th Street or 13th Street, anyway.
It was a basement apartment, that's all I remember.
I never did see the place, but I used to get letters from Bill, especially. Yeah. Bunk hardly ever wrote in those days. When he was on the road, he hardly ever wrote a letter.
But anyway...

It was sort of a tough... almost the edge of Hell's Kitchen, as they called it. Yeah. Farther there on that west side is where the Irish... not that the Irish are necessarily rough, but down here they have the Irish Channel. They have, by reputation, it's supposed to be a tough section for some reason, and Hell's Kitchen, the Irish part of New York is, too. It's a little bit too far south to be able to go ahead and it was a tough section.

Yeah, and it was a tough bar, and I went in and there was Bunk standing at the bar, and I don't know, he was drinking something there, and I guess it was about 2 in the afternoon or 1 in the afternoon. I... this was when I was living at Kratka's, and I was supposed to meet Kratka later on. Bernie de Kratka lived for the... He lived down around the Lancy Street area.
On the east side down there.
Yeah.
I couldn't remember if he was up on 3rd Avenue or someplace. Another friend of ours lived up that way. I forgot.
Harold, I think, or somebody lived up there.
No, another fellow. I can't remember his name. Anyway, go ahead.
I can't remember it.
You're talking about over at the saloon you went to and the... Uh, yeah, so...

...the inner loft bars. Uh, Bunk was standing there and the rest of the people, of course he was the only Negro in the bar, and the rest of the people, these rough types, they seemed to be very hostile toward him, and I was full of apprehension, you know, as I grasped the situation. And it seemed like Bunk was going to overstep the bounds of good judgment, you know, and get himself into some kind of scrape there, so I was a little scared, and I went up to him. And he was telling some kind of story to the bartender and waggling his finger. He'd get very expansive at times like this, and he'd have his hat over on the side. That was his trademark when he was out drinking, he'd have this Homburg cocked over the side, and he'd be standing at the bar waggling his finger at the bartender and telling some kind of story, and I guess he was just getting grunts, you know, and cold stares as a response. But before long, he started talking about different places around the world, and he started talking about some place in Australia. I guess it was one of the big cities, maybe Melbourne or Sydney or one of those places. But he started talking about a hotel or something in that city, and the bartender suddenly became interested, you know, and they got to talking. And it turns out that the bartender had come from that city, and that Bunk knew his mother, you know, and Bunk mentioned her name and described her, and the guy said, Yeah, yeah, that was my mother. Apparently she ran the lounge in a hotel or something, or Bunk had worked for her or something like that. But all of a sudden it was a great warm reunion, you know, type situation, the whole feeling of the thing changed. And everybody was slapping each other on the back, you know, this kind of thing. And Bunk was describing, you know, in perfect detail things about the place that the bartender was saying, yeah, yeah, agreeing with him. And at this point Kratka comes in, and Bunk is feeling particularly playful now, and starts sparring around with Kratka, you know. Kratka is a very well-built guy, very broad shoulders and powerful build, and Bunk was challenging him to a fight, very playfully. Yeah. But the next thing we knew, he was kind of sparring around and throwing a couple punches, you know, and Kratka was just trying to defend himself, and being backed up to a table there. And all of a sudden, the bartender is coming around the bar, and he's warning Kratka not to touch that old man, you know, or he's going to suffer dire consequences. And poor Irv didn't know what to do. He just walked into the place, and it looked like he was going to have the whole clientele on top of him. They were all for Bunk. Yeah, that's right. Don't you dare touch that old man, you know. And Kratka hadn't lifted a hand.
And you actually heard all that talk then yourself about the Australia trip and all that.
Oh yeah, definitely.
Because a lot of people won't believe that Bunk ever left New Orleans or Louisiana, are they, you know, when he talks about being around the world and all that.
It's very strange, the kind of attitude, but...
Actually, something almost similar to that, I understand, I wasn't there to hear it myself, so I have to just take other people's words, it happened with Harry Bridges, you know, in...
Yeah, that's right. Bunk says he remembered Harry Bridges from...

Yeah, and some of his folks too, he knew, I don't know, his family out there in Australia. And evidently, you really did convince him, and I mean, they remembered enough because Harry arranged for him to use the CIO room, you know, for the Sunday program. So I mean, that's not all on somebody's imagination, including Bunk's, I don't think, either.
Well, I mean... But anyway...
Did Bunk ever talk about going any other places, any other countries, like Japan or China or Africa or anything else?

I can't remember that offhand. I can't remember that offhand. The only other place he talked about that I can recall was the little town on the Texas border that he spent some time in. Yeah. And I remember him talking about that. But one thing I should mention before I forget, and that is talking about the lessons, that at one point there he was saying that he would make me another Randy Brooks.
Yeah.

And, of course, at the time, the name Randy Brooks didn't mean anything to me. I mean, I'd heard the name, but I wasn't acquainted with the playing. And, but Bunk was saying that Randy Brooks was one of his best pupils, and I've always... Actually, he didn't teach him, actually. Yeah, he said he taught Randy, and I've always been curious to find out. Yeah, I don't know anything about him, either.

I never met him or heard him, but if I remember rightly, some record company had given him a contract about that time or a year or two before, maybe, and we're going to build him up to be another, say, band of the Tommy Darcy type or something like that. That's faintly in my mind. I'm not sure. I'd have to, we'll have to look that up now.
Yeah. So...
Did he ever talk about any of his other pupils that he... Yeah. Either later old ones that he talked to you about?
But I don't remember hearing anything different about that than what I heard on the Monk Talking records, those three sides that came in.
People like Tommy Ladner and, of course, Louie and different people.

But I do want to say about this episode in the bar that this was a typical example of a kind of playful mood that Bonk would get into with people. He would... He had a very devilish side to his personality when he would, just for the heck of it, he'd start giving somebody a hard time with kind of tongue in cheek. Yeah. But yet he'd make you feel awful uncomfortable for a minute, you know, because you didn't know how to take or how to handle the situation, you know.

Well, you mentioned the other night too that things aren't a typical of Bunky, that maybe argue all night along about some little point that didn't amount to anything, some little funny argument. Yeah. Just for the fun of it.

And then maybe when it was all over... He'd say the opposite. He'd just make one statement and walk away and leave it hanging in the air. Yeah. And you'd realize you'd made a fool out of yourself the whole time. He'd be all twisted up, yeah. He didn't know now whether he was kidding the whole time. He didn't know what to think. Yeah.

He'd do things like that repeatedly, yeah. If I remember the other night you mentioned something, some detail escapes me now about Bechet and speaking about when he helped Louis and all that. That's right.

What was that? Well, there was a time when Bechet was playing at Ryan's and Harold Draub and a friend of mine from Baltimore and myself went into Ryan's to see Bechet and Bunk turned up and he had been drinking very heavily. And he was closer in the disorder that they often got in at such times. And he was sitting at our table and then he'd get up to the bandstand and be singing along with the tune. And he was having some kind of contest with Sidney about what... Trying to name tunes that Sidney couldn't remember. But Sidney seemed to be able to remember everything that Bunk was trying to catch him on, you know. It was very, very good. And they played a bunch of tunes that I never heard before or since. I mean, just really obscure old tunes. And finally, after the evening was over, the five of us went to the cafeteria at Bickford's, I think it was. And it was Sidney and Bunk and Harold and my friend and myself. And Bunk was saying to Sidney, talking about teaching Louis and how Louis was denying that he had taken lessons. And Bunk says, don't you remember Sidney when I was giving lessons to Louis and you would be there? And Sidney says, yeah, you know. And Sidney agreed with him 100% that he had taught Louis.
Actually helped him with his horn.
And that he had taught Sidney too. I don't know how much he taught him, but he said that Sidney agreed that he had been a pupil, a music pupil of Bunk.
Did Bunk and Ply actually help Louis with his horn in addition to just playing for him or letting him follow him?

Well, he said taught him, I mean, and that's what Sidney agreed to, you know. So I got the idea it was lessons, I mean, you know, that they had come to Bunk, you know, to take a music lesson. That's the idea I got. I mean, you might ask Harold about it because he remembers these things more clearly, more verbatim than I do, but I'm sure he would remember this particular episode. He was there then. Yeah. But it was nice to see that Bunk and Sidney had made up too, you know.
Yeah, that was considerably later than their Boston fiasco.

Yeah. He was calling him Sidley, Sidley, and he was talking to him like you talk to a little kid, you know. And Sidney, whose dignity was not accustomed to such a position, was kind of embarrassed. But after a while he just realized he had to take it, so he stood up pretty well. And Bunk accused Sidney of going out with Bunk's girl here in New Orleans back maybe 50 years before, you know. And Bunk says, I know about you. I know that you used to date this girl, you know. And Sidney says, well tell me Bunk. He says, how come you never mentioned it to me before? I said that happened 50 years ago or whenever it was. We thought it was kind of funny, you know. He suddenly comes up with this accusation.
It really had been Bunk's girl then I guess. Yeah, yeah. Sidney didn't deny it either. No, he agreed.

He had been guilty. But he says, how come you never mentioned it to me before? Apparently Bunk never mentioned it to me the whole Boston thing. Yeah. It's a matter he didn't throw it up there when they were arguing all the time.

I had a lot of trouble up there. Is there anything else about any of the other nights that you remember going around with Bunk to hear music or anyplace else that you ran across him? Not necessarily at Lessons or at the Stuyvesant or someplace where he was playing while you're in this groove about like Ryan's or anyplace else. Do you remember Bunk coming in or Harlem or anyplace else?

I remember Bunk playing at Ryan's, playing beautifully at Ryan's. It was a session, I think it was one of the sessions, the Sunday sessions that Lips Page was usually playing and Bunk came in to sit in. And I remember Lips was standing at the bar and was completely moved. Bunk was playing so beautifully and Lips really did love the way Bunk played, you know. And he wouldn't even play. He wouldn't even get on the bandstand. He says, that's the man, you know. He says, I don't want to play. And it was very good. I think Willie the Lion was playing piano then and the Lion was doing a good job. He was playing for Bunk, you know, very well. Played very well together at that time.

We were talking the other night about Bunk in Texas and I think I told you that, if I remember rightly, that Bunk played at the American Theatre in Houston. And Lips Page was sort of a bellboy or a reporter or whatever you'd call it. But they helped him with the baggage in and out. And he always said the two biggest tippers were Bessie Smith and Bunk. I don't know if Bunk ever just came in and out or stayed there all the time. But anyway, evidently Bunk would give him good tips for helping him. I'm quite sure that was Lips Page.
Yeah.

Is there anything about Sammy Price and Bunk? I know they worked together. I can't recall anything offhand. Except of course where you know that Sammy's mother must have been Bunk's girl back in Texas there too. Yeah, yeah. He went out with her up there too, you say.

Yeah, they seemed to be old friends, that's right. Was she working at... She was working at Ryan's at the time. I don't remember her at all. Well, she was a very fine blues singer and she wasn't working entertaining at Ryan's. No, I know. A restroom attendant or something? Yeah, something like that.
I might have seen her but I don't remember seeing her those years.

Well, she had her followers and when a few people would come in that liked to hear her sing, she'd get up and sing with the band and sang very well. I know I never heard her. There was a time when...well, there was this job that we played with Bunk with...I guess it was Al Nicholas on clarinet. And I'm not clear on the personnel because it started out, I think it was a weekly Saturday night dance thing. Kratka himself sponsored this and we had two trumpets and the rest was standard New Orleans instrumentation. And later on it worked into a thing where they had two bands alternating, see, so that the personnel changed slightly. But, uh, the...I don't remember which time it was. There was one time, it might have been the first or second, uh, of these dances that, uh, uh, Bunk wasn't feeling too well. He got there late and, and, uh, he was hardly playing and, and he was telling me, go ahead, you take the lead and you do it, you know, you run the thing. And, uh, I was sweating, you know.
But this caravan, those dances were...was Bunk supposed to be there for all of those or was that your band or what was it? I don't remember. Well, uh...it wasn't there.
It was Kratka's band and, and he hired, uh, uh, Bunk and, and everybody else. Bunk was just, just had that time open and took the job. Yeah.
Bunk was supposed to be there regularly then. Yeah. It wasn't just as a start of special guest once a month or something.

No, well, it was, it was just a once a week thing anyway. Yeah. And, you know, it was like, it was like a jazz concert on a Saturday night with dancing. But, uh, uh, anyway, he told me to, to take over and I, I tried, you know, I did the best I could. But the next week, uh, Papa Mutt was there in the audience and he, he was visiting from, from the West Coast. And I guess he had heard stories about how Bunk was falling down on the job sometimes, you know, and, and he was probably hoping to, that he, uh, maybe be needed, you know, and get a chance to sit in. And, uh, uh, Bunk was playing more strongly than I've ever heard him before or since. I mean, it was a fantastic, uh, lip he had that night. He was, he was, uh, shaking high notes like a big band lead trumpet player, except that he was still had that beautiful tone of his. Yeah. And, uh, uh, I mean, I just, just about didn't blow my horn all night. I was just sitting there with a mouth hanging open and, and, uh, Bunk was playing in a, actually in a slightly different style from the style I'd been used to. It was somewhere between his regular style and Louie's style. Uh, it was, uh, and he was singing tunes. He was really feeling fine. And, and wherever Mutt would be dancing in the room, uh, Papa Mutt's very graceful dancer. Yeah. And, uh, uh, uh, wherever Mutt would be dancing, Bunk's horn would be pointed right, right at that spot, you know. And, uh, it was kind of funny to see that. But, uh, Bunk was just blowing beautifully. And, and I, at some point in the evening I said, uh, Bunk, you're just playing so great, you know. And, uh, he said, well, he says, I'm just paying you back the favor. He says, you filled in for me last week, and so I'm, I'm helping you out this week. He said. You know. He was probably really thinking about Mutt a good deal, too. Yeah, sure, sure. He was just fighting his arm.
Yeah, he was trying to show Mutt how it should sound.

Yeah, well, he, he, he was often putting people on, you know. Yeah. And you just had to, you had to kind of play, play the game with him. Uh, the, the people that, I think, got along best with Bunk were the people that, that could, uh, carry on this playful kind of multi-level, uh, you know, conversation with him. Because it's the kind of thing he liked to do. It's the way he liked to, to, uh, kick it around, you know.
I remember one night that. One night, uh, Sidney.

I, I think I was a little too naive and direct to be able to, uh, you know. I mean, I would take statements too seriously, and finally I'd give up. I kind of exasperated trying to get a straight answer from the guy, you know. Go on. Yeah.

I was going to say, one night, uh, Sidney, uh, Boucher came in, uh, that was 19, uh, the, uh, January of 1946. It had been almost a year since they'd been in Boston together, but they hadn't forgotten any of it. And, but Sidney came up to the Stuyvesant to hear him one night and sat at the table. And Bunk really perked up then and really played about the best of any time. I think I heard him at the Stuyvesant, possibly. One of the best nights he ever had. And he kept the horn pointed right at Sidney then too, most of the night. Yeah. Showing how he could blow. He really could. Sidney, he kept saying, well, I know he can blow. I always didn't say Bunk could play good and nobody was trying to give him any argument. Yeah. Sidney, I don't think it hurt him play that way probably since he was a kid, you know. Certainly not in Boston. Yeah.

Well, now Bunk had his, had his own way of playing, uh, these tunes. He, uh, particularly with the Stuyvesant band, he'd, uh, uh, he'd play a couple ensembles in and then, uh, then George would, uh, come in for a solo usually with Jim, the two of them. And Bunk might even keep playing real quietly. I used to get real close to the, to the horn. He'd point the horn down at the floor. And sometimes he'd just be moving the valves and I knew he was playing something and if only I could hear it. And I don't know, it always seemed to me that the prettiest things he ever played were the things that, that you could hardly hear. Yeah, some of those second hearts. He'd play little phrases that were just unbelievable. He'd wonder, did I hear it or not, you know. And just little turns and, and things. It, uh, it seemed to me he would play things more daring, you know, real quietly than he would loud. He, he, he actually had a very classical approach, a very formalistic approach to playing. And, uh, uh, uh, each chorus was constructed in a very clear, clear-cut way. And, uh, he had a, uh, a counter theme for each, uh, tune that, that he played. He, uh, he had a second theme. And he would play that, uh, generally after all the choruses. In other words, if there's gonna be two or three ensembles out, let's say after the piano chorus, that was the, that was the, the, uh, the comma in the middle of the sentence for that band, it was a piano chorus. And then Funk would, would come in with his, his secondary theme, which was, uh, uh, usually a beautifully conceived thing where it would, it would have pauses in the same places that the original tune had notes and it would have notes in the places where the, you know, the original, it would be a real counter melody, a beautiful counter. And, uh, it would have little turns and, and, uh, he would play that and, uh,
Without anybody else taking the straight melody.

No, sometimes he'd play it as an ensemble lead or sometimes he'd play it as a solo. Uh, yeah, without anybody else playing the straight melody. It would, and, uh, and then he sometimes he used that to take the thing out. In other words, he'd play that for two or three choruses in a row. And sometimes he'd, uh, he'd go to a simpler riff to take the thing out from that. Yeah. And, uh, I, I, one of the few things that I can remember musically was, uh, that had never been recorded, was the, I don't think it had been recorded, was the counter melody he used on Honeysuckle Rose, which was a very, uh, sounds like something Lenny Tristano might have written in Conception. It was very, uh, complex, uh, uh, very fine thing. Uh.
Did you ever hear him where you, uh, thought he was trying to play a Louis chorus or anything?

Well, he had choruses that, that I wondered where it came from. Uh, St. Louis blues, when his lip was, was strong at the Stuyvesant, he'd get up and play the, the four or five successive choruses that I had heard Louis play on St. Louis blues. Uh-huh. And, uh, it sure sounded when he played him like he had invented him. I mean, it didn't sound like he was imitating anybody younger than himself, you know, uh, but, uh, of course it's impossible to tell where it started. Yeah. I, I tend to feel that, uh, because they fit into his style so well that, that they probably were his choruses, unless maybe King Oliver or somebody, uh, back far enough started him and Bunk picked it up.
Yeah, we'll never know now, I guess, actually, what happened.
But the, those traditional St. Louis blues choruses, he, uh, he did play.
Now, the other night you made a remark, uh, sort of a quotation of Bunk, something about that he had to change his style. Well, that's one thing.

I don't, I don't know if he said this to me or if he said it to somebody else and, and they told it to me, but somewhere along the line Bunk was supposed to have said or said that, uh, maybe jokingly, you know, who knows, that, uh, that Louis took his style and so he got a new style. Cause somewhere along the way Louis started playing like him and so he decided to play differently, you know. And of course it, it was said that he was not playing the same style that he had played as a young man that, that, uh, in New York or, you know, on the comeback, uh, his comeback, that he was playing a, uh, somewhat of a different style. Now, I don't, I don't remember where that came from, whether it was Bunk himself that said it, but I remember that, that several of us took it quite seriously and were, hey, we were asking Bunk about it, trying to figure out what he used to play like. Uh, Baby, I think in his book said that, uh, Bunk played a lot, he was surprised that Bunk played so cleanly and he hadn't remembered Bunk, Bunk playing so cleanly. But, uh, maybe it was just, uh, that his, that he organized his, uh, phrases and things more clearly having had a more experience behind him.

Um, I remember, this is another case like you don't, I don't remember if Bunk said it directly to me or the other people that he'd, once as if he'd never changed his style much, that his style always used to be good and it was still good.
Mm-hmm.

In particular, I do remember now that, uh, he told George Sabak, uh, uh, part Egyptian, he sent trumpet player he'd been in California, stopped to see him before any of us did in about 1941, actually heard him play before most of us. And Bunk played Panama for him and told him he played it the same then for him as he always had played it in the old days too. And another occasion, I remember in New York when, uh, remember this young bunch, we used to call it the Scarsdale Bunch with Bob Wilbur and, uh, what's his name, Glazel? Johnny Glazel, yeah. Johnny Glazel. Johnny Glazel. And they, uh, George Lewis was going up to their house and some of the other fellows baby up, had been invited up to Scarsdale. They didn't, if they did invite Bunk, he never went, you know. Mm-hmm. Somebody was telling me that Johnny played just like Bunk, same style. And Bunk, he was ridiculing that idea, he said, how can he play my style? He said, I've got a dozen different styles I play.

Yeah, well that's the truth actually. How can he play my style? Yeah. Bunk, I don't know if you call them completely different styles, but Bunk certainly had different facets to his playing in different situations, quite different from each other. And, uh.

Did you ever hear Baby and Bunk together in that last trip that he made in 47 there, you know, with the caravan days? I know they played once or twice with Pops Foster, maybe with Hodes or somebody down on someplace like the Roseland or one of those other Arcadia ball, some other ballroom there, right off of Broadway, I think. I don't remember. A special thing one night. Did you hear him?

I don't remember. I know we had two bands toward the end of that caravan engagement. Maybe Baby was the other drummer. Uh. Toward the end we split the thing into two bands, and I think Bunk had one band. Bunk was a trumpet for one band and I was a trumpet for the other. I think we split it up that way. Uh. And, uh. So maybe he was playing with Baby then. I seem to recall that he was. I think he might very well might have been. I think, unless I'm getting all this mixed up together now, I think maybe Cy St. Clair might have been on tuba.
Well, did you ever hear Mutt, uh, change the subject, did you ever hear Mutt play in New York that engagement? Uh. That, uh, that, uh, year. I think I heard Mutt sit in, I believe, somewhere.

Uh, I don't remember where it was, but he sat in some place. I don't know if it was, uh, at the Stuyvesant, uh, during the dances that, uh, Harold, uh, gave, or, uh, with the band that Bunk recorded with later on, you know. Uh. Uh. It might have been there. I think Mutt showed up there too.
Uh. Well, uh, to change the subject again, speaking of horns, I just happened to think about it, uh, did Bunk ever say and make any remarks about his Selmer trumpet, if he liked it, or?

I think he liked it. He certainly handled it as if he liked it, but, uh, he tried my cornet. I was playing a King cornet at the caravan one night, and, and, uh, he sounded kind of different on the thing. And, uh, we were all very interested, you know, to hear, uh, how he sounded on it. And, uh, he, he liked the horn. He, he, he said he thought it was a very fine horn. Maybe there was just nostalgia for, for playing a cornet. Maybe he just, uh, actually wanted to be playing a cornet the whole time.
I understood he always wanted the con cornet, actually, because we got him the Selmer thing at a bargain without knowing that it wasn't his favorite and all that, too.
Well, he sure got a nice sound out of that Selmer. Yeah. I mean, it, uh.
Did he use your mouthpiece when he played it? Yeah, I guess he did. He had to, I guess.
Well, it was, I, I imagine it was similar to, to the one that he was using. I was using pretty stupid.

He had an old French mouthpiece, a Cuesnone, I can't pronounce it, C-U-E-S-N-O-N. Oh, yeah. And, uh, had a new shank, an old cornet mouthpiece, and he had a new, uh, Rudy Muck put a new shank on it and replated it. Mm-hmm. So he couldn't tell what it was, but I think he always used that most of his late years. Mm-hmm. Did he ever give you any advice on mouthpieces? No. On mouthpieces?

No. No, he never did. I, I, uh, I thought the mouthpiece he had looked kind of standard, as I recall, the looks of it. I think so. It looked like about a, could have been a ten, ten and a half C Bach, uh, mouthpiece. Mm-hmm. From the looks of it.
It wasn't extra deep, but it certainly wasn't shallow, as I remember.
No, I don't think it was a cushion rim type thing.
No, not a big rim or anything, as I can remember. Dave Bell has that, I guess.
Oh, is that right? He still has the horn. I'm sure he'd never get rid of it.
Did Bunk ever give you any advice about breathing or anything else?
No, he never talked about breathing. He, uh, uh, he, uh, just told me to get my own style and… What about vibrato?
Uh, we forgot to touch about that. Yeah. We can run out of tape here in a minute, too. If you have him a second, you can tell about… Well, I…

Did he use finger vibrato or a lip vibrato? No, he… I never saw him shake the horn. He, uh… He, uh… He used a breath vibrato sometimes. I'm sure it came from the diaphragm, and then there were other times… Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
You were talking about vibrato, you were talking about his...

Yeah, well, I was very interested to see. Vibrato is a funny thing. It's... On records, fast vibrato doesn't usually sound very good. I've noticed Sidney Vachey's vibrato on records doesn't have the same effect that it has in person. Yeah, but in person, when you can hear this full rich tone, the vibrato just seems to enhance it completely and you don't get any of the unpleasant illusions that you get on a record. And the same thing is true of Bunk's vibrato. In person, it was just the most beautiful sound. Yeah, that's true. The record that sounds like Bunk's vibrato in person was, to me, is the record that Mitchell made of Some Rainy Day, I think, where he's holding long notes and... Jimmy Noon?
